title: Why does a Spring Boot `MultipartFile` upload fail once the file exceeds ~1–10 MB (`MaxUploadSizeExceededException` / `SizeLimitExceededException`), what are the default limits (`spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size` ≈ 1MB and `max-request-size` ≈ 10MB), how do you raise them (those properties, or a programmatic `MultipartConfigElement`/`MultipartConfigFactory`), and why is simply raising the limit the WRONG answer for truly large uploads — stream the `InputStream` instead of buffering the whole file in memory (to avoid OOM), and prefer direct-to-object-storage (presigned URL) or chunked uploads?
shortTitle: Why does a Spring Boot MultipartFile upload fail past a few MB, what are the default limits, how do you raise them, and why is raising the limit the wrong fix for truly large uploads

s1_definition.profdef: Spring Boot applies two multipart limits by default, `spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size` at about 1 MB per file and `spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size` at about 10 MB for the whole request, and exceeding them throws `MaxUploadSizeExceededException` (wrapping the servlet container's `SizeLimitExceededException`). You raise them with those properties or programmatically via a `MultipartConfigElement` built from a `MultipartConfigFactory`. But raising the number is the wrong answer for genuinely large files, because `MultipartFile.getBytes()` buffers the entire file in heap, so large uploads cause OutOfMemoryError under concurrency. The correct approach is to stream the file's `InputStream` to its destination without buffering, and for very large files to bypass the application server entirely using presigned direct-to-object-storage uploads or chunked uploads.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India's online form has a small letterbox slot, big enough for a one-page form (1 MB) and a whole envelope of pages (10 MB total). When Rajesh tries to post a thick 50 MB loan file, it does not fit and gets rejected with a "too large" notice. You can widen the slot (raise the limits), but if you make it huge and a thousand customers all shove thick files through at once, the mailroom floor (heap memory) is buried under piles of paper and the whole branch collapses. The real fix is not a bigger slot but a conveyor belt that carries each page straight to the warehouse as it arrives (streaming), or better, giving customers a gate pass to deliver straight to the warehouse themselves (presigned URL).
s1_definition.oneliner: Defaults are ~1 MB per file and ~10 MB per request; raise them with properties for modestly larger files, but for truly large files stream the InputStream or go direct-to-storage, because getBytes buffers the whole file in the heap.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spring Boot applies two multipart limits by default, `spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size` at about 1 MB per file and `spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size` at about 10 MB for the whole request, and exceeding them throws `MaxUploadSizeExceededException` (wrapping the servlet container's `SizeLimitExceededException`). You raise them with those properties or programmatically via a `MultipartConfigElement` built from a `MultipartConfigFactory`. But raising the number is the wrong answer for genuinely large files, because `MultipartFile.getBytes()` buffers the entire file in heap, so large uploads cause OutOfMemoryError under concurrency. The correct approach is to stream the file's `InputStream` to its destination without buffering, and for very large files to bypass the application server entirely using presigned direct-to-object-storage uploads or chunked uploads.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India's online form has a small letterbox slot, big enough for a one-page form (1 MB) and a whole envelope of pages (10 MB total). When Rajesh tries to post a thick 50 MB loan file, it does not fit and gets rejected with a "too large" notice. You can widen the slot (raise the limits), but if you make it huge and a thousand customers all shove thick files through at once, the mailroom floor (heap memory) is buried under piles of paper and the whole branch collapses. The real fix is not a bigger slot but a conveyor belt that carries each page straight to the warehouse as it arrives (streaming), or better, giving customers a gate pass to deliver straight to the warehouse themselves (presigned URL).

**One line to remember:** Defaults are ~1 MB per file and ~10 MB per request; raise them with properties for modestly larger files, but for truly large files stream the InputStream or go direct-to-storage, because getBytes buffers the whole file in the heap.

sections.s2_technical:
Why it fails. When a browser or client posts `multipart/form-data`, the servlet container (Tomcat under Spring Boot) parses the parts. Spring Boot's autoconfiguration sets guardrails so a single huge or malicious upload cannot exhaust server resources by default. The two limits are `max-file-size`, the maximum size of any one uploaded file, defaulting to roughly 1 MB, and `max-request-size`, the maximum size of the entire multipart request including all files and form fields, defaulting to roughly 10 MB. When an upload exceeds either, Spring throws `MaxUploadSizeExceededException`, which wraps the container's `SizeLimitExceededException` or `FileSizeLimitExceededException`. If you do not handle it, the client gets an ugly 500; you should catch it in a `@ControllerAdvice` and return a clean 413 Payload Too Large.

How to raise the limits with properties. In `application.yml` you set:

```yaml
spring:
  servlet:
    multipart:
      max-file-size: 50MB
      max-request-size: 60MB
```

This lets a 50 MB file through, with a little headroom in the request size for form fields and boundaries.

How to raise them programmatically. Sometimes you need to compute limits at runtime or you are not using the property path. You define a `MultipartConfigElement` bean built from `MultipartConfigFactory`:

```java
@Bean
public MultipartConfigElement multipartConfigElement() {
    MultipartConfigFactory factory = new MultipartConfigFactory();
    factory.setMaxFileSize(DataSize.ofMegabytes(50));
    factory.setMaxRequestSize(DataSize.ofMegabytes(60));
    factory.setFileSizeThreshold(DataSize.ofKilobytes(256)); // spill to disk above this
    return factory.createMultipartConfig();
}
```

The `fileSizeThreshold` is important: below it, the part is kept in memory; above it, the container spills the part to a temp file on disk instead of holding it in the heap. Raising the threshold too high reintroduces the memory problem.

Why raising the limit is the wrong answer for truly large files. The tempting fix is to set `max-file-size: 5GB` and move on. But the real danger is how the file is consumed. If your controller does `byte[] data = file.getBytes();` or `file.getBumptedContent()` style, you load the entire file into the heap as a byte array. A 5 GB file is 5 GB of heap for one request; a handful of concurrent large uploads is an instant OutOfMemoryError that crashes the whole JVM, taking down every other user's request with it. So the limit is not the real constraint, memory is. Raising the limit without changing how you read the file just converts a clean 413 rejection into a catastrophic OOM crash.

The correct approach when the file must pass through your service: stream the `InputStream`. Instead of `getBytes()`, you call `file.getInputStream()` and copy it in fixed-size chunks to the destination, such as `StreamUtils.copy(in, out)` or `Files.copy(in, targetPath)`, or pipe it to an S3 `PutObjectRequest` using `RequestBody.fromInputStream(in, contentLength)`. Only one chunk is in memory at a time, so memory stays bounded no matter how large the file or how many concurrent uploads. You still cap total size to prevent abuse, but you do it with a streaming-aware guard, not by buffering.

The best approach for genuinely large files: do not pass bytes through your service at all. Use presigned URLs so the client uploads directly to object storage, or chunked/multipart uploads for multi-gigabyte files. Then the `max-file-size` property is irrelevant because the file never becomes a `MultipartFile` on your server; your API only handles small control requests. This is the architecture that actually scales.

The senior nuance is matching the tool to the size. For small files like a profile photo or a one-page PDF, a `MultipartFile` with a modestly raised limit and streamed `getInputStream()` is perfectly fine and simplest. For tens or hundreds of megabytes, stream and consider WebFlux for concurrency. For gigabytes, always go direct-to-storage with presigned multipart. Blindly raising the limit on a buffering controller is the anti-pattern.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India lets customers upload supporting documents. Rajesh (SAV2001) uploads a 40 MB scanned loan packet; the online portal serves thousands of customers during a loan campaign.

Problem 1 — the upload failed at 1 MB with a confusing 500 error. The default `max-file-size` of 1 MB rejected Rajesh's 40 MB file, and the uncaught `MaxUploadSizeExceededException` gave him a stack trace instead of a clear message. This is why we raise the limit sensibly and handle the exception to return a clean 413.

Problem 2 — after raising the limit to 5 GB, the server crashed with OutOfMemoryError. The controller read the whole file into a byte array with getBytes, so a few hundred concurrent 40 MB uploads buried the heap. This is why we must stream the InputStream instead of buffering, so memory stays bounded.

Problem 3 — even streaming, a customer's 3 GB archive still tied up a thread for minutes and risked disk fill. This is why truly large files should bypass the service with a presigned direct-to-storage upload.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo of the decision logic and streaming copy: a `MultipartLimits` holder, a `MultipartExceptionHandler` mapping to 413, an `UploadHandler` that streams small/medium files chunk-by-chunk (bounded memory) and routes large files to presigned direct upload. It processes a 40 MB streamed upload and a 3 GB direct-upload routing decision, and shows the 413 path for a file over the cap.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's 40 MB PDF, Priya's 3 GB archive, and a 6 GB file.

Step 1: Rajesh's 40 MB enters the handler. It is under the 5 GB absolute cap and under the 50 MB direct-upload threshold, so it takes the streaming path.

Step 2: streamToStorage reads the InputStream in 8 KB chunks and writes each chunk to storage before reading the next. At any instant only 8 KB is in memory, so even with hundreds of concurrent 40 MB uploads the heap stays tiny. The outcome is STREAMED.

Step 3: Priya's 3 GB enters the handler. It is under the 5 GB cap but over the 50 MB direct threshold, so instead of passing bytes through the server the handler mints a presigned URL and returns DIRECT_PRESIGNED. Priya's client will upload straight to S3; the server never touches the 3 GB.

Step 4: The 6 GB file enters. It exceeds the 5 GB absolute cap, so the handler throws PayloadTooLargeException before doing any work. In the real service the @ControllerAdvice turns this into a clean HTTP 413 rather than a 500 stack trace.

Step 5: Contrast with the broken approach: had the controller called getBytes on Priya's 3 GB, the heap would have tried to allocate a 3 GB byte array, and a few concurrent such uploads would have thrown OutOfMemoryError and crashed the JVM for everyone. Streaming and direct-upload both avoid that.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Rajesh outcome: STREAMED — streamed 41943040 bytes, heap stayed bounded
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Priya outcome: DIRECT_PRESIGNED — client uploads straight to S3: https://nbi-docs.s3.amazonaws.com/CUR3001/archive.zip?X-Amz-Signature=SIM
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [SEVERE ] 413 rejected: massive.iso size 6442450944 exceeds cap 5368709120
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Upload request (userId, filename, size)
    │
    ▼
  UploadHandler.handle()
    │
    ├─ size > 5GB absolute cap? ──YES──▶ PayloadTooLargeException ─▶ HTTP 413
    │
    ├─ size > 50MB direct threshold? ──YES──▶ mint presigned URL
    │                                          │ client PUT bytes DIRECT to S3
    │                                          ▼  (server never sees bytes)
    │                                     S3 nbi-docs
    │
    └─ else (modest file) ──▶ STREAM InputStream
            │ read 8KB ─▶ write 8KB ─▶ read 8KB ...  (O(8KB) memory)
            ▼
       storage (bounded heap, safe under concurrency)

  ── Contrast: the WRONG way ──
  getBytes() → allocate whole file in heap → 3GB × N concurrent → OutOfMemoryError → JVM crash
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Spring Boot MultipartFile upload fails past a few megabytes because Spring Boot applies two default guardrails: max-file-size, about one megabyte per file, and max-request-size, about ten megabytes for the whole multipart request including all files and form fields. When an upload exceeds either, Spring throws MaxUploadSizeExceededException, which wraps the servlet container's SizeLimitExceededException, and if I do not handle it the client gets an ugly five hundred error. The first fix is to catch that exception in a ControllerAdvice and return a clean four-hundred-thirteen Payload Too Large so the client understands what happened.

To actually allow bigger files I raise the limits, either through the properties spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size and max-request-size in application.yml, or programmatically by defining a MultipartConfigElement bean from a MultipartConfigFactory where I also set a file-size-threshold so that parts above that size spill to disk instead of sitting in the heap. That is fine for modestly larger files like a forty-megabyte scanned packet.

But simply raising the limit is the wrong answer for truly large files, and this is the key point I stress. The real constraint is not the configured number, it is memory. If my controller consumes the file with getBytes, it loads the entire file into the heap as a byte array, so a single five-gigabyte file is five gigabytes of heap for one request, and a handful of concurrent large uploads is an instant OutOfMemoryError that crashes the whole JVM and takes down every other user. Raising the limit on a buffering controller just converts a clean rejection into a catastrophic crash. We hit exactly this: after bumping the limit to five gigabytes, a few concurrent forty-megabyte uploads buried the heap because the code called getBytes.

So the correct approach, when the file must pass through my service, is to stream the InputStream. Instead of getBytes I call getInputStream and copy it to the destination in small fixed-size chunks, or pipe it straight into an S3 PutObject request with RequestBody.fromInputStream, so only one chunk is in memory at a time and memory stays bounded no matter how large the file or how many concurrent uploads. And for genuinely large files, gigabytes in size, the best answer is to not pass the bytes through my service at all: I mint a presigned URL so the client uploads directly to object storage, or use chunked multipart uploads, which makes the max-file-size property irrelevant because the file never becomes a MultipartFile on my server. The principle I give an interviewer is that I match the mechanism to the size, raise limits and stream the InputStream for modest files, and go direct-to-storage with presigned multipart for large ones, because the limit is a guardrail and memory is the real constraint.
